findings.claim: effective_value and describe_source independently re-implement the same layered-precedence policy, and they have drifted: effective_value tests presence with `key in env` (so an explicit empty-string override counts as the layer carrying the key, per the module docstring's stated contract), while describe_source tests truthiness with `env.get(key)` (so an explicit empty-string override is treated as absent and falls through to the next layer). For a key set to "" in env, effective_value returns "" (env), but describe_source reports "project", "user", or "default" instead of "env" -- the --explain output would name the wrong layer, contradicting the value effective_value actually used.
findings.source: settings.py:18 `if key in env:` vs settings.py:28 `if env.get(key):` (same drift repeats at lines 20/30 for project and 22/32 for user); contract stated at settings.py:5-7 `A layer "carries" a key when the key is present, whatever the value -- an explicitly empty string is a deliberate override, not an absence.`
findings.remedy: Stop expressing the precedence policy twice. Add one internal helper, e.g. `_layer_for(key, env, project, user)` returning the layer name using presence (`in`) checks per the documented contract, and have both effective_value and describe_source call it (the latter mapping the returned layer to its value or to "default"). This removes the duplicate-authority split rather than just patching describe_source's checks in place.

findings.claim: The three-layer test/lookup order is asserted a third time, independently of the two if-chains, by the module-level `ORDER` tuple -- but ORDER is never referenced by effective_value, describe_source, or the test file, so it cannot enforce or even signal the drift between the two functions it appears to document.
findings.source: settings.py:14 `ORDER = ("env", "project", "user")` -- not read anywhere else in settings.py or test_settings.py
findings.remedy: Either wire ORDER into the lookup (iterate it in effective_value/describe_source instead of hardcoding the chain) or delete it. A constant that describes a policy but isn't consulted by the code implementing that policy is a third place to keep in sync and is the same drift risk as the effective_value/describe_source split.

findings.claim: No test exercises an explicit empty-string override, even though the module docstring calls out that exact case as the reason presence (not truthiness) must be used. The drift between effective_value and describe_source is invisible to this suite.
findings.source: test_settings.py:1-38 (all five tests use non-empty string values for env/project/user); contract at settings.py:6-8
findings.remedy: Add a test that sets a layer's value to "" and asserts both effective_value returns "" and describe_source names that same layer -- this is the test that would have caught the drift in finding 1.

findings.claim: column_subset and should_encode each unwrap a Packed kind to its primitive with the identical expression (`col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind`), duplicated verbatim rather than shared. The module docstring explains why encode_categoricals bypasses column_subset (it expresses its own column set via should_encode), but that rationale justifies not sharing the *set-membership* logic -- it doesn't explain duplicating the *kind-resolution* logic, which both functions need identically and would need to change together if a second wrapper type were added.
findings.source: columnstore.py:53 `alias = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind` vs columnstore.py:63 `kind = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind`
findings.remedy: Extract a one-line helper, e.g. `def _primitive_kind(kind: str | Packed) -> str: return kind.primitive if isinstance(kind, Packed) else kind`, and call it from both column_subset and should_encode. Minimal ceremony, no new class or seam, and it removes the one policy (how to resolve a column's primitive kind) that both functions must keep in sync.

findings.claim: CHANGES.md asserts the should_encode refactor is behavior-preserving for every kind column_subset used to pick up, but the test suite never constructs a column with kind "masked_text" or Packed("masked_text") -- one of the three categories should_encode's own docstring names. The equivalence claim for that kind is asserted, not verified.
findings.source: CHANGES.md:7-10 `every column kind that used to be picked up ... is still picked up here, and nothing else is`; test_columnstore.py:1-53 has no occurrence of "masked_text"; should_encode's category set at columnstore.py:64 `return kind in {"text", "masked_text", "choice"}`
findings.remedy: Add a masked_text column (plain and Packed) to the test fixture and assert it's encoded, matching the coverage already given to text and choice.
